title: Writing Production-Grade Dockerfiles
summary: The patterns that separate a hobby Dockerfile from one you'd trust in production.

slides.markdown:
A hobby Dockerfile just needs to work. A production Dockerfile needs to be **small**, **fast to rebuild**, **safe to run**, and **free of leaked secrets** — none of which happen by accident.

The good news: it's a fixed checklist, not a deep art. Multi-stage builds, careful instruction ordering, a non-root user, and a `.dockerignore` cover the vast majority of what separates the two.

slides.subTitle: Compile in one stage, ship a slim runtime
slides.markdown:
A **multi-stage build** uses one stage with the full compiler/build toolchain to produce an artifact, then copies only that artifact into a second, minimal stage that actually ships:

```dockerfile
FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN go build -o /app

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
```

The final image contains only the compiled binary — no Go toolchain, no source code, no build-time dependencies — often shrinking a multi-hundred-MB build image down to tens of MB.

slides.subTitle: Distroless vs Alpine vs scratch
slides.markdown:
| | `scratch` | Distroless | Alpine |
|---|---|---|---|
| Contains | Nothing at all | A minimal runtime, no shell/package manager | A full but tiny Linux distro (shell, `apk`) |
| Debuggable in-container? | No | Barely (no shell) | Yes — you can `exec` in and use a shell |
| Best for | Fully static binaries (Go, Rust) | Production images where you don't need a shell | When you still want easy in-container debugging |

**How to decide:** reach for distroless or scratch for the smallest attack surface in production; keep Alpine (or a full base) for images you still need to poke at directly.

Order instructions from **least likely to change** to **most likely to change**: base image, then OS-level dependencies, then language dependency install (from a lockfile copied in *before* the rest of the source), then the application source itself last.

Getting this order right means a routine code change only invalidates the last one or two layers, keeping most rebuilds down to seconds instead of minutes.

Containers run as **root by default** unless told otherwise — meaning a process that escapes the container's isolation inherits root privileges on whatever it escapes into. A `USER` instruction switches to an unprivileged account before the container's main process runs:

```dockerfile
RUN adduser -D appuser
USER appuser
```

This is one of the highest-value, lowest-effort security changes available: it costs two lines and meaningfully shrinks the blast radius of a container-escape vulnerability.

slides.subTitle: Speed and secrets
slides.markdown:
`.dockerignore` excludes files from the build context sent to the Docker daemon — same idea as `.gitignore`. Skip `node_modules`, `.git`, build artifacts, and local `.env` files, and two things improve: the build context uploads faster (less to send to the daemon), and secrets or bulky junk in your working directory can't accidentally end up baked into a layer via a broad `COPY . .`.

A missing `.dockerignore` is a common way a `.env` file with real credentials silently ends up inside a shipped image.

| | Floating tag (`node:18`) | Pinned version (`node:18.20.3`) or digest |
|---|---|---|
| Reproducibility | Can silently change underneath you | Byte-identical every build |
| Convenience | Automatically gets patches | You control when updates happen |
| Risk | An upstream change breaks your build with no code change on your side | You must actively track and apply security patches |

**How to decide:** pin exact versions (or digests) for production builds so nothing changes without your knowledge, and manage upstream updates deliberately through your own dependency-update process, not passively via a floating tag.

slides.subTitle: Turning a bloated Dockerfile into a multi-stage one
slides.markdown:
Before: one stage that installs build tools, compiles, and ships everything — often 900MB+.

```dockerfile
FROM node:18
COPY . .
RUN npm install && npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

After: a build stage plus a slim runtime stage — typically under 150MB.

```dockerfile
FROM node:18 AS build
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:18-slim
COPY --from=build /dist ./dist
COPY --from=build /node_modules ./node_modules
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

**Wrong belief:** "I'll `RUN` a command with a secret, then `RUN rm` it later — it's gone."

**Why it's wrong:** each `RUN` creates a new layer, and layers are additive — a later `rm` only hides the file in the merged view, not the earlier layer, which still ships inside the image. Anyone with the image can extract that layer and recover the secret.

**Correct model:** never let a secret touch a layer — use build-time secret mounts (`--mount=type=secret`), or inject secrets at runtime via env vars or a secrets manager instead.

slides.subTitle: Dockerfile-level vs orchestrator-level
slides.markdown:
A Dockerfile `HEALTHCHECK` runs a command on an interval and marks the container `healthy`/`unhealthy` — useful standalone, since plain Docker otherwise only knows if a process is *running*, not whether it's actually serving traffic correctly.

Once you're on an orchestrator like Kubernetes, its own readiness/liveness probes take over this job with far more control (what to do on failure, how to gate traffic) — the Dockerfile-level check becomes redundant, and most production setups drop it in favor of the orchestrator's probes.
